newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds firm in line with European markets.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds firm in line with European markets.

text.p: Irish bonds firmed in line with other European markets on Tuesday despite general worries over European Monetary Union (EMU), dealers said.

"Surprisingly, given the backdrop, Irish bond prices were marked up in line with Germany today," a dealer said. "A possibility for this is that the German government looks like it's going to hammer out a deal with the Bundesbank on gold revaluation."
Also, dealers surmised, a potentially EMU-negative victory by the Socialists in the second-round of the French general election at the weekend had been "at least partially priced in by the market".
By 1515 GMT the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 20 pence at 102.10 to yield 5.93 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 53 pence at 109.23 to yield 6.62 percent.

Dealers said that yields against German bunds were broadly unchanged from the previous close, with the yield against Germany at 144 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 89 over in the 10-year.

Sources in the Bonn coalition said earlier that it may be willing to forego plans to revalue the central bank's reserves in 1997, a scheme the Bundesbank opposed saying it would jeopardise the stability of economic and monetary union.
The French Socialists, meanwhile, have said they want more specific employment commitments in Europe as well as a broader EMU.
They are also considered unlikely to push through any extra measures in this year's budget in order to reduce the fiscal deficit to meet the Maastricht criteria.
"It's probably the case that a lot of this market-unfriendly news was priced in, limiting damage," a dealer said. "If anything it's hit currencies much harder than bonds."

European markets may also have been buoyed by better sentiment in the U.S. overnight amid speculation that the U.S. payroll number, due on Friday, might be lower than the consensus because of technical factors.
Looking ahead, dealers said, Ireland's borrowing requirement figures, due tomorrow, and credit numbers due on Thursday would be of interest to the Irish market.
